title: Red Urine and a Crusted Nose / Test the Kidneys Today, Refer Urgently

blocks.text: Red Urine and a Crusted Nose / Test the Kidneys Today, Refer Urgently

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-26 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 2) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min · Guidelines: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (Kidney Int 2024;105(3S)) · Related AMaC: Consultation: acute kidney injury on an ACE inhibitor and NSAID

Dear Doctor, a 61-year-old school secretary. Two weeks of red urine, blocked and bleeding nose, cough and tiredness. Creatinine 310 µmol/L (was 80 last year). BP 158/96. Please assess and advise. She has consented to see you.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Blood in the urine, a crusted nose and a rising creatinine suggest ANCA vasculitis, a kidney emergency: test the kidneys today and refer urgently.

The Examiner Trap. She thinks it is a water infection and a sinus problem. Candidates give antibiotics and send her to her GP. Pass: dipstick, repeat kidney function, same-day renal referral, and do not wait for a biopsy. Fail: antibiotics and discharge.

rows: Infection or vasculitis? Get the story.
"Tell me about the red urine and your nose. Any cough, blood in the phlegm, joint pains or rashes?"
Introduce, consent, ask about pain; urine, nose, cough, haemoptysis, joints, rash, drugs, fever.
Is she unwell, and what organs are involved?
"May I check your blood pressure, nose, chest, skin and legs?"
BP, nose, chest, skin, joints, oedema, urine dipstick.
"This may be an inflammation of your blood vessels affecting your kidneys. I'd like your kidney tests today."
Dipstick, repeat urea, creatinine and potassium, ANCA, urgent renal referral.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are. A 61-year-old school secretary. Worried, tired, a little breathless. Lives with your husband.
Opening line. "I think it's a water infection. My nose has been blocked and bleeding too."
Volunteered. Red urine for two weeks; crusty bleeding nose for months; tired.

Only if asked. Never smoked; alcohol rarely; no recent travel; no regular tablets and no allergies. Your sister has been on dialysis for diabetic kidney disease. A dry cough; you coughed up a little blood once. Aching knees and wrists. No rash. Fever last week. No weight loss. Ibuprofen a few times for the aches. No kidney disease before. You do not drive today.
Hidden concern. Your sister is on dialysis and you fear the same. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Is it a water infection?" "Will I need dialysis?" "Do I need a biopsy?" "Can I go home?"
How you react. Good handling: you agree to stay. Poor handling: if sent home on antibiotics you say you feel fine and leave.

Findings (released as each step is done). BP 158/96, pulse 90, oxygen saturation 94 per cent in air (scenario values). Crusted nasal mucosa with old blood. Chest clear. Knees and wrists tender, no swelling. No rash. No oedema. Urine dipstick blood 3+, protein 2+. Creatinine 310 µmol/L (scenario).

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): ANCA vasculitis with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Q2 Investigation (R6): repeat kidney function, urine protein ratio, ANCA, anti-GBM, chest imaging. Q3 Action (R6): urgent renal referral; urgent renal assessment; with a compatible clinical picture and positive MPO or PR3 ANCA, do not delay treatment for biopsy, especially if deteriorating (KDIGO 2024). Q4 Treatment (R6): glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide (KDIGO 2024). Q5 Plasma exchange (R7): specialist consideration with creatinine over 300 micromol/L, dialysis requirement, rapid creatinine rise or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with hypoxaemia; also ANCA and anti-GBM overlap (KDIGO 2024).

Curveball 1. "Give antibiotics for a urinary infection." (R6) Safe: dipstick shows nephritic pattern; infection and other mimics still require assessment, but this nephritic pattern and rapid renal deterioration demand urgent renal review.
Curveball 2. "She coughs up blood and her oxygen falls." (R6) Safe: alveolar haemorrhage; urgent resuscitation and senior help.

Curveball 3. "Biopsy before treating." (R6) Safe: do not delay specialist treatment for biopsy in rapidly deteriorating, clinically and serologically supported ANCA vasculitis; biopsy remains important when feasible.
Curveball 4. "I'm going home." (R7) Safe: she has capacity; explain risks; offer a safety net.

CANDIDATE: What's happened? [R1 Fail] (No cough or joint history. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Reports a rash and oedema that are not there. [R4 Fail])

Examiner note: No history, signs invented, wrong diagnosis. Sending her home on antibiotics with a creatinine of 310 µmol/L and haematuria is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): her kidneys can fail within days.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello. May I examine you? Any pain or breathlessness? I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Tell me about the red urine and nose. Any cough, blood in phlegm, joint pains, rash or fever? What medicines do you take, including painkillers? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: I coughed up blood once. My sister is on dialysis; I'm afraid.
CANDIDATE: That's a real worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Checks BP, nose, chest, skin and joints; dipsticks urine. Reports blood pressure 158/96 and crusting in the nose. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This looks like an inflammation of the blood vessels affecting the kidneys: ANCA vasculitis. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I'll repeat your kidney tests and potassium today, send an ANCA test, and refer you urgently to the kidney team. Please avoid ibuprofen. [R6 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I recommend staying in for tests and treatment. The alternative is going home, but that risks your kidneys failing. What would you like me to explain further? Thank you. [R7 Pass] [R1 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear. Did not name alternatives or discuss treatment and biopsy.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: Hello. May I examine you? Any pain or breathlessness? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Tell me about the red urine and nose. Any cough, blood in phlegm, joint pains or rash? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? Are you comfortable? Would you like a drink of water? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any numbness, eye problems, weight loss or previous kidney disease? [R2 High]
PATIENT: My sister is on dialysis.
CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. We're acting today to protect your kidneys. [R3 High]
(Checks BP, nose, chest, skin and joints; dipsticks urine. [R4 High])
(Neurology and fundi normal; no rash, oedema; chest clear. [R4 High])
CANDIDATE: Vasculitis is most likely; anti-GBM disease, lupus and infection are alternatives I'll test for. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll repeat your kidney tests and potassium today, send an ANCA test, and refer you urgently to the kidney team. Please avoid ibuprofen. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: I'll add a urine protein ratio, anti-GBM and a chest film, and the kidney team may start treatment without waiting for a biopsy. If creatinine rises quickly they may discuss plasma exchange. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: Options: admission and treatment, a biopsy, or doing nothing, which risks kidney failure. Treatment includes steroids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. What would you like me to explain further? [R7 High]
Examiner note: Answered the fear of dialysis and covered treatment and biopsy.

R6: Sending her home on antibiotics with haematuria and a creatinine of 310 µmol/L is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): kidney failure can follow within days.
R2: Not asking about haemoptysis misses lung involvement.
R4: Reporting a rash not present shows signs were assumed.
R5: A urinary infection does not explain nasal crusting and cough.
R7: Instructions without options leave her without a say.
"Have you coughed up blood?"
"I'd like your kidney tests repeated today."
"What worries you most?"
KDIGO 2024: diagnose ANCA vasculitis as early as possible; waiting for kidney biopsy should not delay immunosuppression in rapidly deteriorating patients (practice point 9.1.1).

Induction is glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide (recommendation 9.3.1.1, grade 1B); consider plasma exchange for creatinine above 300 micromol/L, rapidly rising creatinine or dialysis need, and for alveolar haemorrhage with hypoxaemia (practice point 9.3.1.9).

This is a renal emergency with possible pulmonary–renal syndrome. Arrange admission and same-day nephrology review, stop NSAIDs, check for hyperkalaemia and do an ECG if potassium is high, serial renal function, potassium, urine microscopy and protein quantification, MPO/PR3 ANCA, anti-GBM, complement and relevant infection tests. A clear chest does not exclude alveolar haemorrhage. Immunosuppression is specialist-led after evaluating infection and mimics; biopsy should not delay it in rapidly deteriorating supported disease. KDIGO 2024 plasma-exchange consideration includes creatinine above 300 micromol/L, rapid rise or dialysis, hypoxaemic alveolar haemorrhage and anti-GBM overlap.
THINK: Vasculitis; rapidly progressive kidney injury.
SAY: "This may be inflammation of your blood vessels; I want your kidney tests today."
DO: Cough, haemoptysis, joints; BP; dipstick; ANCA; renal referral.
NUMBERS: Creatinine 310 µmol/L (was 80), BP 158/96 (scenario).
TRAP: Antibiotics and discharge.
FINISH: Admit; renal team; treat without waiting for biopsy.
